trials.label: r1c1
trials.name: 1-epoch high-throughput recipe
trials.hypothesis: ppo_epochs=1 raises the budget to about 106k steps. Using 128 envs × 16 steps gives about 52 updates and about 1,660 minibatch steps (64 samples each). lr 2e-3, ent_coef 0.002 and clip 0.25 let the policy sharpen quickly. More fresh designs should matter more than reusing samples on this task, which needs generalisation. Refuted if dev success stays near 0 on both seeds while the 2-epoch variant clearly beats it.

"""Starting architecture: the main campaign's default policy (conv encoder, width 64, depth 2, ReLU,
no normalisation), rewritten as a candidate file. A 3x3 conv body, a 1x1 conv placement head
(one logit per brick type and anchor cell), and DONE and value heads on mean+max pooled features."""
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

WIDTH = 64
DEPTH = 2


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        layers, c_in = [], spec.in_channels
        for _ in range(DEPTH):
            layers += [nn.Conv2d(c_in, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()]
            c_in = WIDTH
        self.body = nn.Sequential(*layers)
        self.place_head = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, spec.n_types, 1)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, WIDTH), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.body(obs)
        place = self.place_head(f).flatten(1)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)


RECIPE = {'lr': 0.002, 'n_envs': 128, 'rollout_len': 16, 'n_minibatches': 32, 'ppo_epochs': 1, 'ent_coef': 0.002, 'gamma': 0.97, 'gae_lambda': 0.9, 'clip_eps': 0.25}

trials.label: r1c2
trials.name: 2-epoch balanced recipe
trials.hypothesis: ppo_epochs=2 gives about 60k steps (29 updates of 128×16) and about 1,860 minibatch steps. It reuses each sample a little while keeping data diverse. lr 1.5e-3, ent_coef 0.003, gamma 0.97. This tests whether a small amount of sample reuse beats pure throughput. Refuted if it does clearly worse than the 1-epoch recipe (by more than about 5 points over both seeds) or stays at 0.

trials.label: r2c1
trials.name: 1-epoch, 64 envs, more updates
trials.hypothesis: This keeps r1c1 but uses n_envs 64 (16 minibatches of 64). That doubles the number of policy updates to about 104, each collected on fresher data, with the same total samples and gradient steps. With a single epoch, fresher rollouts should reduce off-policy drift and speed up learning in a budget-limited run. Refuted if dev success is clearly below r1c1's 0.068 (for example under 0.04).

trials.name: 1-epoch, max learning rate
trials.hypothesis: This keeps r1c1 but raises lr from 2e-3 to 3e-3, the maximum allowed. Training is clearly limited by the budget: train success was still rising, and moving from defaults to a faster recipe was the biggest gain so far. The linear decay to 0 and gradient clipping at 1.0 should keep the late phase stable. Refuted if dev success falls clearly below 0.068 or collapses on a seed, which would mean the run is unstable rather than too slow.

analyses.1: No trials yet. The starting recipe gets 0/512 on all three seeds, so it is almost certainly limited by budget, not by luck. With 4 PPO epochs the budget is 32,768 steps. That is only 8 updates and roughly 1,000 episodes, far too few to learn exact builds of 8–20 bricks. Cutting ppo_epochs is the main lever. With 1 epoch the budget becomes about 106k steps, more than three times the data. Smaller rollouts give more policy updates, minibatches of 64 keep the number of gradient steps high, and a higher learning rate suits the short schedule. Exact success needs a sharp policy that stops at the right moment, so a lower entropy coefficient should help greedy evaluation. A slightly higher gamma helps credit the +1 bonus for an exact build. Both proposals test a high-throughput recipe; they differ in epochs, learning rate and gamma.
analyses.2: Changing only the recipe moved dev success from 0.000 to 0.068 (1 epoch) and 0.061 (2 epochs). Small batches (128 envs × 16 steps, 64-sample minibatches), a high learning rate and low entropy are what made the network learn at all. The gap between 1 and 2 epochs is within noise. Still, 1 epoch gives about 1.8× more fresh designs (106k vs 59k steps) at a similar number of gradient steps, and it reached much higher train success late in training (0.072 vs 0.026). That suggests fresh data and fast learning matter more than reusing samples. Training takes only about 20 s, so time is not a constraint. The agent is clearly still learning fast when the budget runs out, so the most likely gains come from learning faster. With one round left, I refine r1c1 along two separate lines: more frequent policy updates, and a higher learning rate.
